The shingles vaccine (Shingrix) is recommended for everyone over 50 and is a 2-dose series. It is publicly covered in Ontario for ages 65-70; many private plans cover it otherwise.
Most common side effects are redness and soreness at the injection site; occasionally flu-like symptoms for a day or two (more common with the second dose).
The benefit is a reduced risk of developing shingles and - importantly - reduced risk of complications such as persistent nerve pain (post-herpetic neuralgia).
If you would like to proceed, let me know which pharmacy to fax your prescription to; the second dose is given 2-6 months after the first. If you have questions, please book an appointment to review.

S – Subjective

CC: Rough, bumpy skin on [upper arms/thighs/cheeks].
HPI: Chronic, asymptomatic or mildly pruritic follicular bumps; gradual onset; worse with dry/cold weather. No pain, drainage, or systemic symptoms.
Associated symptoms: Denies significant erythema, swelling, or signs of infection.
PMHx: Atopic dermatitis, xerosis, or other skin conditions [if applicable].

Patient concerns: Cosmetic appearance, skin texture, or itch.
O – Objective

Skin: Multiple small, rough, follicular keratotic papules over [bilateral upper arms/anterior thighs/cheeks], with or without mild perifollicular erythema.
Skin may be dry; no pustules, drainage, or significant tenderness.
No evidence of secondary infection.
Distribution and morphology consistent with keratosis pilaris.
A – Assessment

Keratosis pilaris – benign, chronic follicular keratinization disorder.
Typical clinical presentation; no investigations indicated.
Differential diagnosis if atypical: folliculitis, eczema, or other follicular eruptions.
P – Plan

Education/reassurance: Benign, non-contagious condition; common and often improves with age. May fluctuate with season and skin dryness.
Skin care:
Apply fragrance-free emollient regularly, especially after bathing.
Use gentle cleansers and lukewarm water; avoid harsh scrubbing and picking.
Topical treatment if desired for persistent roughness:
Urea 10–20% cream, lactic acid 10–12%, or salicylic acid 1–2%; start gradually as tolerated.
Counsel regarding irritation, dryness, and discontinuation if significant irritation occurs.
Avoid keratolytics on broken or inflamed skin; use caution on the face and in children.
Follow-up: Reassess in 6–8 weeks if symptoms persist or treatment is desired; consider dermatology referral for diagnostic uncertainty or refractory, bothersome disease.
Return precautions: Seek reassessment for new pain, pustules, drainage, marked redness, or rapidly changing lesions.
